overview: The imported “Arawaks” record covers eastern Caribbean islands. Arawakan is a language-family term, not the name of one island empire, and these communities should not be equated with mainland Lokono Arawak. Archaeological sites below illuminate regional life without proving each settlement’s language. The 800 to 1400 boundaries do not mark a people’s beginning or extinction.

periods.title: Interconnected island communities
periods.summary: Late Ceramic Age settlements adapted to changing coasts and maintained regional relationships.

periods.title: Colonization and resistance
periods.summary: European invasion disrupted Indigenous networks; communities faced displacement and continued adapting.

periods.title: Living communities
periods.summary: Dominica’s designated Kalinago Territory became a continuing center of communal life and government.

items.text: Arawakan languages of the islands were not all the same. Historical Island Carib speech belonged to this family but differed from Taíno and mainland Lokono. People also used Cariban vocabulary and speech registers, making colonial labels a poor guide to simple ethnic boundaries.

Dugout canoes carried people between islands to visit relatives, maintain alliances and exchange goods. Pottery, basketry, ornaments, tools and foods moved through these networks. A stretch of sea could connect neighbors rather than separate two isolated worlds.

Early colonial exchange brought glass beads, metal tools and European ceramics into existing island networks. It also accompanied enslavement and the arrival of devastating infections. The movement of objects therefore records both new encounters and a deeply unequal transformation of Caribbean life.

At Anse Trabaud on Martinique, wet mangrove deposits preserved wood and plant remains that usually decay. Investigators studied layers dated approximately 660 to 1170 CE. Mud that made excavation difficult also protected small details of people’s daily surroundings.

Starch studies of tools and pottery at Anse Trabaud identified maize, beans, manioc, arrowroot and cocoyam in older deposits. The tested later objects yielded a narrower selection. The evidence reveals varied food preparation, while sample differences prevent a complete menu for every household.

Anse Trabaud residents appear to have moved toward higher beach barriers as their shoreline changed. The researchers link settlement organization with shifting lagoons, rising sea levels and severe weather. Choosing where to rebuild a home was part of adapting to an unsettled coast.

At Anse à la Gourde in Guadeloupe, later houses had round or oval plans. Builders drove some posts deep into bedrock and secured others with stone slabs. Strong foundations mattered where powerful storms could put a home’s construction to a very serious test.

Studies of Caribbean teeth found differences in diet and dental disease between communities. Many people ate substantial plant carbohydrates, and increasingly processed foods left changing patterns of wear and cavities. Archaeologists can learn about meals from the teeth that once chewed them.

Some teeth also show wear associated with holding materials during work. Researchers connected particular marks with activities such as cord-making or basketry in part of the studied population. A mouth could act as an extra grip when two hands were already busy.

A documented later written name is “Waitukubuli”, translated “tall is her body”, for Dominica. The country’s biodiversity plan prints both name and meaning, referring to the mountainous island. This Kalinago place-name witness belongs to later written documentation; no deciphered local script is established here for 800 to 1400.

In Dominica, Kalinago territorial land is communally owned and administered through a council consisting of a chief and six other elected members. This continuing government is one specific community’s institution, not the survival of an imagined single Arawak empire.

A Kalinago community report describes planting about 9,000 food and forest trees in 2022, with more than 150 families participating. Farmers also received support for cassava production. Caring for watersheds, growing food and passing on knowledge remain connected activities.

ending.text: The map’s 1400 cutoff is not an extinction date. European colonization later disrupted island societies and networks, while Indigenous descendants continued building new lives and institutions. Kalinago communities remain part of the eastern Caribbean’s present as well as its history.
